CHARLE-TON, June 3 — A special to the News and Courier says a colored man named Caleb Campbell, who had been fully identified as having attempted a criminal assault on Mrs. Martha Rainson on Wednesday, May 24, near Blythewood, in Fairfield county, was taken from the jail at Winnssboro last night by a party of disguised men and hanged about three miles from there. A Midnight Tragedy. THE WORK OF THE LYNCHERS IN FAIRFIELD COUNTY. Caleb Campbell Taken from Jail at Winnsboro' and Hanged.
WINNSBORO, June 3, 1882.

As already telegraphed to the News and Courier on Wednesday afternoon, May 24th, an outrageous assault was committed upon the person of Mrs. Martha Rains, the wife of Mr. James A. Rains, near Blythewood, in this county. The circumstances attending the assault have been detailed, and are briefly these: About sundown on Wednesday evening Mrs. Rains went to the spring near her house to get a bucket of water. After she had filled her bucket and was about returning to the house, Caleb Campbell, a colored man, approached her, threw his arms about her neck, and dashed her to the ground. Mrs. Rains resisted, cried for help, and after struggling on the ground for five or ten minutes, the negro left without accomplishing his villanous purpose, being frightened away by sounds of an approaching wagon.

As soon as the news of the assault was known in the community a number of persons were arrested and brought before Mrs. Rains for identification. When Caleb Campbell was brought before her he was instantly identified as the person committing the assault. He was taken before Trial Justice D. Hogan on last Monday, and after a preliminary examination was regularly committed to jail for trial at the next Court of Sessions for this county, which will be convened on next Monday. The public were greatly incensed at the outrage and many threats of lynching were made.

In order to prevent a resort to popular violence Campbell was brought to Winsboro' on the train on Monday night, in charge of a special constable, and safely lodged in jail. Last night, between 12 and 1 o'clock, a party of about eighty men rode into Winsboro', and going to the jail told the sheriff they had a prisoner for him. Not suspecting that anything was wrong the sheriff opened the door, when he was seized by several men and roughly thrown to the floor. On trying to summon help a saddle cloth was thrown over his head to prevent any outcry. In spite of the sheriff's protests and resistance his pockets were searched and the key secured to the door leading to the third story of the building where the cells are situated. A number of the men went up stairs and examined the cells asking at each cell who occupied it. They forced open the cell in which Campbell was confined. As soon as he was led out into the corridor a pair of iron handcuffs was promptly clasped around his wrists and he was taken out of jail into the street and mounted on a mule, in front of one of the vigilance committee.

A rope was placed around Campbell's neck and the crowd went at full speed down the Columbia road to a point about three miles below Winnsboro'. There the mule on which the prisoner was mounted was ridden under a large post oak tree, and the rope around his neck was thrown over a convenient limb. The mule was then led out and Caleb was left hanging between heaven and earth.

As soon as the sheriff was released he went to the intendant of the town, J. J. Neil, for counsel and assistance, and as soon as he could get his horse saddled, set out with a deputy in pursuit of the raiders. On passing Major T. W. Woodward's residence, about three miles from Winnsboro', the sheriff stopped and called for help. Major Woodward joined the sheriff and went down to the spot where Campbell was hanging. Major Woodward examined the body and found no signs of life and he and the sheriff cut the rope and lowered the body gently to the ground.

At the inquest to-day, after examining a number of witnesses, who testified to the material facts as related above, the jury, of which Mr. J. H. Cummings was foreman, rendered a verdict that "Caleb Campbell was killed and murdered by hanging by some person or persons to the jury unknown."

The Higher Law. On Friday night Caleb Campbell was taken from Winnsboro jail by a party of men and hanged by the neck. The crime attempted by him and frustrated only by accident, was the most grievous in the whole calendar, ranking in its ferocity and beastliness more highly even than murder. We have frequently expressed the opinion that there is but one case in which lynch law is justifiable. The case of Caleb Campbell was the one calling for
the interposition of this higher law. The crime was not consummated, but the devilish purpose was in his heart. So that though under the cold, unsympathetic provisions of the statute law, he could only have been imprisoned, yet every instinct of the human heart revolts against any punishment less than death for such abandoned beasts. The victims of such assaults should not be compelled to undergo the ordeal of testifying in the courts, as this would be additional torture. The higher law steps in and avenges outrage by swift retribution.

Let it be known, once for all, that in Fairfield the white beast or the black beast who strikes at virtue and chastity will swing as surely as the crime is proven and as soon as a rope and a tree can be found strong enough to bear his weight.

MATTERS AT RIDGEWAY.
The Growing Crops, and the Farmers' Expectations--The Business Outlook, and the General Prospect.

Correspondence of the Columbia Register.

RIDGEWAY, June 2.—The hard rain and wind of Wednesday afternoon—a rain hard to beat in quantity of water falling per minute—did considerable damage to the farmers by blowing down their small grain. The frequent showers are not favorable to the harvest season, upon which we have fully entered.

Muscle and a knowledge of how to throw a cradle and tie a bundle of grain are at a premium now. None need lounge in the market places these spring days pleading "no man hath hired us."

The reaper has not visited this section yet. Farmers are afraid of it until they can see it in successful operation. One farmer has bought one, but rumor says he is in the same fix with it that the farmer was in who spent a rainy day trying his luck as an amateur clock tinker. After he had taken the old family clock to pieces he found that, put it together as he would there was one wheel too many.

The report of the farmers about the grain crop is that it is good—a large acreage and an abundant yield. The wheat prospect is better than a few weeks ago. Rust is confined to the blade and on many farms the blade is spared.

Cotton chopping is about over in some places, but in others—the larger portion too—much cotton is unchopped. It looks well since sunshine and shower has superseded the untimely cool weather, which insisted on taking spring from us. The lint prospect is much improved.

Corn looks well. A man about five miles from Ridgeway is talking about laying by some. Not much corn in the country, I ween, so far advanced as that. The planters here cut outs are not heavy corn planters. The lien victim, of course, has no option, but those who can do somewhat as they think best say oats pay much better.

Good gardens are plentiful and are a subject of beast. Several claim to be in the superlative.

Business is dull except on Saturdays. This shows that the farmers stay at home and attend to their crops. They seem to be in good spirits and speak cheerfully of the prospect. No fault of labor, seasons or soil is comparable to the credit system as a barrier to agricultural prosperity. To buy corn and meat at the present high cash prices is financial ruin to the farmers, but to buy these indispensable articles at the rate charged by the supply merchant on time is to sell themselves and their land for bread, and they and their lands will be servants unto Pharaoh. Some few farmers are rising above this state of things, and it is to be hoped that fair seasons and a good crop will place a large number of them beyond the necessity of buying on credit at all and all of them beyond the necessity of buying on a ruinous credit. We

must not look upon the supply merchants as harpies devouring the best of the banquet and returning curses in answer to protestation. The better part of them wish that business were on a cash basis, but times being as they are they make the best of them. These are not times for vituperation, but for retrenchment and reform.

BONNIE SWITZER.

JUDGE LYNCH IN FAIRFIELD.—A few days since a shocking account was published setting forth the attempted outrage of a young married lady, Mrs. Martha Raines, on May 24th, in the neighborhood of Doko by a negro fiend. The wretch was defeated in his purpose by the desperate resistance of the lady, who suffered painful injuries in the encounter. She bit the hands of the negro so severely that when, shortly afterward, she made known the facts to the neighbors and pursuit was made, he was readily identified, and proved to be a negro named Caleb Campbell, of bad reputation in the neighborhood.

Campbell was carried before Trial Justice Hogan at Doko, who committed him to jail at Winnsboro to await his trial at the next term of the Court of General Sessions.

On Friday Judge Lynch's Court assembled somewhere, and the evidence was heard, which left no doubt that the negro Campbell had attempted the foul outrage, and it was decreed that he should be hanged. On Friday night at about 12 Sheriff McCarley was summoned to the door of the jail by two or three men, who stated that they had a prisoner from the country whom they wished to lodge in the jail. The Sheriff dressed himself and came out of the door to receive the prisoner, when he was confronted by a large force of men, whom he could not recognize, and the keys of the jail were demanded at the muzzle of their revolvers. Upon his attempting to raise his lantern to endeavor to see if he could recognize any of the party they warned him that his life would be forfeited on any attempt at recognition or alarm. The party then entered the jail, forced the cell in which Campbell was lodged and brought him out. He was carried by the party, who were mounted, about three and a half miles below the town to the neighborhood of the derrick at Woodward's and there hung to a tree until he was dead, when he was cut down and left under the tree, where he was found by sheriff McCarley and his deputy, who followed in pursuit.

The whole proceeding was so quietly and promptly executed that few persons in Winnsboro knew anything of the occurrence until yesterday morning, when, of course, it produced intense excitement. Large numbers visited the spot and viewed the dead body, and at about 1 o'clock the Coroner held an inquest and found that Campbell came to his death at the hands of some persons to the jury unknown. The body was buried yesterday afternoon on the spot where it was found. — Columbia Register, Sunday.

A TERRIBLE TRAGEDY.
Miscegenation in Randolph County Leads to Murder.
A White Woman Runs Away with and Marries a Negro, Who Kills Her Father in a Quarrel, and is Then Hung by a Mob.
Special to the Register.
W. Va. January 28.

PHILIPPI, W. Va., January 28.—A clandestine marriage between a negro named Luckey, and a white woman named Collins, both of Randolph county, which took place a short time since, has resulted in a terrible tragedy.

The facts, so far, as your correspondent has been able to gather them, are as follows: Collins, the father of the girl, who is a widower, had been paying attention to a young lady named Kelly, who belongs to one of the best families of Randolph county, but meeting with opposition from the young lady's parents, he attempted an elopement, but was pursued and overtaken at Bilington, in this county, arrested and taken back to Beverly.

Enraged at his disappointment he provided himself with a pistol and prepared for war against the Kellys, declaring that he bad been induced to the futile attempt by the importunities of the girl.

While Collins was thus engaged, and absent from home a large portion of the time, his daughter hastily sought her dusky lover, and in a short time they were on their way to Maryland, the nearest Gretna Green. They passed through this place one day last week, apparently as happy as turtle doves, and passed the night a short distance from town at a country inn. They reached Maryland in due time and were married, and without further loss of time returned home.

No sooner had the news of their return reached the ears of the girl's father than he forgot his own troubles in the new disgrace, and made the newly wedded pair the objects of his wrath. On Friday he visited them for the purpose of inflicting condign punishment. A quarrel ensued, when the negro drewa revolver, and shot Collins dead on the spot. The news of the death of Collins spread rapidly in the neighborhood, and in a short time a crowd of hardy mountaineers were on the spot. They wasted no time in useless ceremony, but overpowering the assassin, took him to the woods immediately in front of the cabin, and strung him up to a convenient limb, and left him hanging there. F.

THE BANDOLPH LYNCHING. Additional Facts Concerning the Actors in the Tragedy.
The murder and subsequent lynching in Randolph county last Friday, particularized in yesterday's Register, were generally canvassed at the Capitol yesterday, especially among members and gentlemen from that portion of the State. Superintendent Butcher, Col. Cresap, Prosecuting Attorney Scott and other Randolph gentlemen were all familiar with the actors in the terrible tragedy, and from them the reporter gathered many additional facts of interest.

Collins, the murdered man, came originally from Tennessee, passing into Wayne, thence to Randolph from Upshur. There were two brothers of them, and both of them bore the worst of reputations. Their blood is tainted with an admixture of dusky indian, which accounts for their wild and lawless disposition. Upon their arrival at Randolph, each was accompanied by three or four women. Their faith was apparently Mormon, though it is believed neither was married. The now murdered man had six or seven children. He claimed to be a widower, and has paid attention to a young lady named Kelly, though his reputation made him detestable to the lady's parents. Collins ran off with Miss Kelly, but was arrested and brought back, which caused a deathless enmity between the families.

Calvin C. Luckey, the negro who was lynched, was a young mulatto, well known all over the county, and generally liked. He was the illegitimate son of Bess Luckey, a white woman, and his father was a colored man known only as "Old Baz." He was made much of by the white people, until he finally grew to regard himself as good as they. He was a prepossessing-looking man, a Hercules of strength, and a fine shot. He shunned his own race and sought white companions and at last began to pay attention to a young girl named Yahl. Her father, however, would have none of it, and at the mouth of a rifle drove Luckey away. The latter then turned his attention to Miss Collins, and while her father was prosecuting his own love affair in the Kelly direction, the colored Lothario got into the good graces of the girl. He persuaded her to elope with him and seek some State whose statute books bore no miscegenation laws, and off they went. In several days they returned, claiming to be married; but this was not believed and public sentiment would have driven them out of the county had not the tragic occurrence happened.

But at this time Collins, who was warring with the Kelly's turned his attention to home matters, and shouldering his rifle, started for Luckey. The negro, with Collins' rifle covering him, so the story goes, drew a revolver and instantly killed his father-in-law. Already wrought up by the miscegenation, the mountaineers of Randolph took the law into their own hands and hung Luckey to the nearest tree.

The Randolph gentlemen now in the city are of the opinion that of Luckey and Collins, the negro was the better man. The people out there, however, would not tolerate the inter-race marriage, and to that the lynching is attributable. These gentlemen all say Luckey was a respectable character, and of good repute in the county, but he was spoiled by association, and greatly overestimated himself. In appearance he was a light mulatto, a large, powerful man, with long and only slightly curled hair. And those who knew him seem satisfied that Collins must have come at him with leveled rifle to have tempted him to murder.

A Marriage and Two Murders.
One day last week a ginger-bread negro arrived in this city in company with a fine-looking white girl, and asked a minister to marry them. They were informed that miscegenation was unlawful in this State, and that they would have to go to Pennsylvania. They took the train to the State line, across the mountain to Wellersburg, where they were married. The next day they passed through here on their way to Randolph county, in West Virginia. The girl's name was Collins, and she is of a respectable family. Her father, who resided at Beverly, heard of the whereabouts of the couple, and sought them out. The negro expected to he shot, and drew his revolver and killed Collins. The news spread like wildfire, and soon the negro was in the hands of a mob, who strung him to the nearest tree. The new-made wife is now a widow and an orphan.

St. VALENTINE'S DAY.—The valentine is playing its part just now. The day of Cupid and his capers arrived Tuesday of this week and the little missives, comical and sentimental, principally the former, have already begun to circulate through the mails. The origin of St. Valentine Day is lost in antiquity, and can now be only speculatively fixed. One theory is that it sprang from the ancient Roman Festival of the Lupercalia, celebrated on February 15th. This was at first a shepherd's invocation to the God of Fertility. As young Rome grew the festival became general among all classes, and a college of priests especially devoted to the service of the god was established. When the Christian Church gained power an effort was made to abolish the heathen feast, which by that time had become a mere expression of gallantry; but this proving vain, the date was changed to the birthday of St. Valentine —February 14th. This saint was canonized soon after his execution by order of the Emperor Claudius, about 270. He was a christian Bishop, and he was made the patron of the day, because of the loving charity of his character. Another theory is that the festival, in its essential, if not in its precise date, is as old as the human race, being an expression of the vernal impulse common to all living beings. Reference to the mating of birds in the spring, and to the feelings of love which thrill the breast at the season when nature wakes from her winter sleep, are scattered through all literature back to the earliest times. One day last week a gingerbread negro arrived in this city in company with a fine looking white girl and asked a minister to marry them. They were informed that misegegenation was unlawful in Maryland, and that they would have to go to Pennsylvania. They took the train to the state line, across the mountain to Wellersburg, where they were married. The next day they passed through here on their way to Randolph county, West Virginia. The girl's name is Collins, and she is of a respectable family. Her father, who resided at Beverly, heard of the whereabouts of the couple and sought them out. The negro expected to be shot, and drew his pistol and killed Collins. The news spread like wild fire, and soon the negro was in the hands of a mob who strung him up to the nearest tree. The new made wife is now a widow and an orphan.

He was met by a BAZOO reporter, and in reply to the question as to whether there was anything new, said there was not. Last Saturday night a week ago Marshal Still, of Holden, arrived in Sedalia, having fled from home to escape the wrath of a mob who had sworn vengeance upon him.

A half-witted fellow named Emery, who had been arrested for making insulting propositions to a little girl only twelve years of age, had been taken from the jail and cruelly beaten, and it was supposed that Still and his friends were implicated, and Emery's friends vowed they would have satisfaction.

CONDENSED TELEGRAMS.
A GENERAL order from headquarters of the army provides for a reciprocal crossing of the international boundary line by troops of the United States and Mexico in pursuit of hostile Indians.

N. W. CLAYTON, Territorial Auditor, committed a murderous assault upon J. M. Goodwin, a Tribune reporter, in Salt Lake City, Utah, on the 10th. Clayton is said to have recently gone to polygamy, and after careful investigation the facts were published. Visiting the Tribune office, he denied the polygamy, but admitted he had left his wife, though still supporting her. He undertook to explain his connection with the second as of a purely friendly and business character, and invited Goodwin to call on Mrs. Clayton No. 1 and get her statement. The reporter went to see her, but hardly got into the house when Clayton, in a furious rage, tried to draw a pistol, threatening to kill him, and probably would have carried the threat into execution had not a friend interfered while Mrs. Clayton hurried Goodwin away.

A MOB of twenty-five men, near Lampasas, Texas, the other night, captured George Porter, who was found in possession of a horse supposed to be stolen. His body was riddled with bullets and left on the roadside.

A PREMATURE explosion at Cornwall, N. Y., on the 10th, killed four negro track-layers and wounded several others.

In a collision on the I. B. & W. R., near Springfield, O., on the 10th, Conductor Jas. McNary, was killed and a brakeman and engineer seriously injured. A number of passengers were severely injured. A number of passengers were severely injured.

JAMES DOYLE, aged 14, was shot dead by John Maguire in New York City on the 10th. Maguire is a dog-catcher, and Doyle and other boys stoned him while he was gathering up their pets. The murderer escaped.
BANNOCK Indiana attacked a party of hunters in the Sierra Nevada Mountains, the other day. J. B. Bruner, Thomas Ray, and Samuel Newton were killed.

A New York bride devoted the last few minutes before starting on her bridal trip to revising the proof of the newspaper account of her wedding.

At Dallas, Texas, on Thursday a colored boy placed a can of kerosene in the stove in mistake for a can of coffee. An explosion followed, killing the boy and blowing the house down.

Three foolish young fellows undertook to dance at the grave of a former young companion a few days ago at Lawrenceville, Ill. The friends in attendance drove them from the cemetery, and arrangements were subsequently made to lynch them. Becoming alarmed, the young men attempted to make their escape in a leaky boat, and after having traveled down the river several miles the boat sank, and they were compelled to swim ashore. The night was cold, and their dead bodies were found next day at a point near where they had landed.

Mrs. Sarah H. Dorriss, of St. Louis, who was murdered recently by her vagabond grandson, was the only woman in this country who ever made slave trading a business. She made a large fortune before the war buying and selling slaves, and was estimated to be worth half a million of dollars.

A maiden lady of Charlotte, Michigan, who amassed a fortune as a milliner, built a row of business houses in that city which she has named "Old Maid's Block."

Lieutenant Hayes, who lost his life with General Custer at the time of that fearful Indian massacre, left two orphan sisters, who are now in Washington in destitute circumstances. They have been making underclothes for ten cents apiece in order to buy bread.

While a party of young men were firing a salute at Lancaster in honor of the Democratic victory in that city on Tuesday a week, the cannon exploded, instantly killing Frank A. Herzog and dangerously injuring Peter Roehrich. The latter's right leg was torn off, and he is not expected to live. Both men were married.

Mrs. Elizabeth Treadwell Weston, of Greenfield, N. H., celebrated her one hundred and fourth birthday a few days ago. She was married at eighteen and had twelve children, of whom four are now living. Her oldest son and his wife celebrated their golden wedding a few years ago.

A mass of earth, weighing at least fifty tons, fell upon Joseph Shaffer in the O'Donnell quarry at Tredyffrin, Chester county, a few days ago. His whole body was covered, with the exception of a small space over his mouth, through which he breathed. After thus being confined in great agony for nearly one hour he was released.

Marylanders are sometimes precocious. A lad of seventeen and a girl of fourteen were married recently. The youthful bride had not long before obtained a divorce from her stepfather, who is sixty-five years old.

The discovery is reported of a "rich gold bearing belt" in Chilcot county, British Columbia, above the sixtieth parallel of latitude, just back of the Alaska line.

Henry Hall (colored) of Akron, O., has just been reunited to his mother, brothers and sisters in a truly remarkable manner, and after many years of separation. Hall was born in New Orleans, his mother then being a slave of a Mr Bott. They were subsequently sold to Gov Alcorn of Mississippi. George C. Gotting of San Francisco, suspected that his wife was in love with another man, and by means of a decoy letter induced her to go to a place where she supposed her lover would meet her. There she found her husband instead, and he cruelly stabbed her to death, as well as the infant that she held in her arms. Gotting was convicted and sentenced to be hanged. Mary E. Willis belonged to a church choir, and every Sunday afternoon she went with some city missionaries to sing in jail. She met the condemned wife murderer, and it was soon noticed that she carried him a bouquet at every visit. Love letters were next exchanged, and a few days ago the couple were married in the doomed man's cell. The bride is educated, refined, and has considerable money, which she will spend in endeavoring to gain a new trial for her husband.

In the campaign of 1872 the republican management in this state expended $4000, all told. Not a dollar, so far as we know, went to buy a voter, but the state was thoroughly organized, public meetings were numerous, and documents were freely circulated. The campaign was conducted on a plane of intelligence and patriotism, without a corrupt or sordid element. The result was, the republicans swept the state by 5000 majority. What has been the tendency since? Double, treble, quadruple the amount of money has been used in many campaigns, and never has the republican majority been so large since. Money has been poured into the state by thousands; town upon town now relies upon money solely, and discards public meetings; a venal class of voters and politicians exists all over the state in both parties alike. Men who would scorn to taint themselves in other respects, seem to think that the corrupt use of money in elections is no taint. Where is this thing to stop? We can go on paying our court to men of wealth, because they will "contribute well to the party funds," and we can continue to make ourselves responsible for sowing the seeds of corruption and demoralization, but let us not delude ourselves with the flattering unctions that we are not at the same time corrupting the youth about us, wrecking our own party, and undermining republican government itself.— [Nashua Telegraph.

CALIFORNIA.
Dastardly Attempt to Murder.
ATNONVILLE. January 31 — A most
Dastardly Attempt to Murder.

WATSONVILLE, January 31. — A most dastardly attempt to murder—and probably a successful one—was made near here night before last. It was the occasion of a wedding at the house of Charles Bossi, in the redwoods about eight miles from Watsonville. Bossi had decided to make it a grand affair, had laid in a bountiful stock of wine and whisky, and had caused bonfires to be kindled all around the little house in the Redwood canyon, in order that the many guests should be accommodated. Among those who went without invitation was a gang of toughs from Whisky Hill, a little village about a mile and half from here. It had not been the programme to have dancing, but as many desired to dance a fiddler was sent for. During the dancing the hat was passed around, and these toughs refused to contribute, and were notified by Bossi that those who did not pay could not dance. They thereupon went outside and began to fire off their pistols, some of the shots striking the house. Charles Bossi went out and told them if they did that any more he would make a prison of it, and as he turned to go in one Jose Tejada stabbed him in the back with a dirk. The knife passed between the sixth and seventh ribs into the lung. An Indian who had been teaming for Bossi, named Jilliao, jumped forward and shouted that a man who would stab another in the back was a coward, or words to that effect, at which a brother of Tejada struck him over the head with a pistol and then shot him, the ball ploughing a furrow over the top of the scalp. The surgeon who was called to the case says that Bossi is probably mortally wounded. The doctor does not consider the other man injured very badly. Bossi is a steady, hard working man, and not in the least quarrelsome or overbearing. Jose Tejada has only been out of San Quentin about two weeks. Deputy Sheriff John Gaffey and a posse are scouring the country for him, and it is said that if he is found by any other than the Sheriff's party he will be swung up to the most convenient tree.

LATER — The wounded man is resting a little easier to-day, but the surgeon says the chances are decidedly against him.

SAN FRANCISCO, Jan. 7. — Savage and Alpha are each assessed 50 cents.

A Tombstone dispatch says the stage coach from Tombstone to Bisbee was attacked yesterday afternoon by five robbers, who opened fire with rifles without warning. The driver whipped up the team, and Wells-Fargo's messenger, armed with a Winchester rifle, kept up a running fight with the highwaymen until they headed the coach, which then surrendered. The treasure box containing $6,500 was taken. The passengers were unmolested, and no one was hurt.

A Sacramento dispatch says that Wm. G. Douglass, Postal Route Agent, was arrested to-day for robbing the mails. He was held to answer in $3,000 bail. He ran on the route between San Francisco and Sacramento, via Stockton. Letters for some time on that route have been tampered with. His detection was accomplished by marked letters and money. Douglass confessed the crime.

Charles A. Henry, former editor of the Valkgrin, a Scandinavian journal published in this city, has been engaged by Henry Villard to bring five or ten thousand Scandinavians to engage in the construction of the Northern Pacific Railroad. Inducements will be offered these immigrants to settle on the line of the road.

CASTROVILLE (Cal.), Jan. 7.—Constable John P. Casady and G. Tomassini, in a Swiss saloon, got into a fight to-day, during which Casady shot and killed his opponent. Both had pistols. Casady claims to have acted in self-defense. Tomassini quarreled with him because Casady was recently instrumental in having him convicted of violating the Sunday law.

WATSONVILLE (Cal.), Jan. 7.—Deputy Sheriff John Gaffey and posse arrived here to-day after five days' hunt in the mountains after the men connected with the recent attempt to murder Chas. Rossi. Being informed about 2 o'clock this morning that a certain Mexican had concealed the fugitives, they compelled him to disclose their hiding place, which was in the hollow stump of a large tree, by stringing him up until he was nearly choked to death. The posse then surrounded the stump and demanded their surrender. They were answered by a pistol shot, and then firing opened on both sides. One of the desperadoes was shot, probably mortally, but made a dash and escaped temporarily in the darkness. The other, Ignacio Tejada, then surrendered, and was brought to town, but was run off under guard on the Santa Cruz train to avoid lynching.

WATSONVILLE, January 7th—For five days.
Outlaws Captured in a Hollow Tree—A Desperate Fight.

WATSONVILLE, January 7th.—For five days Deputy Sheriff John Gaffey and posse have been scouring the mountainous country for miles around the Loma Prieta for the men who were connected with the attempt to murder Charles Rossi. Gaffey and his men have been going night and day, and have only had a few hours sleep during the time they have been out. This morning about half-past 8 they arrived in this town with four prisoners, having had a desperate fight in the mountains at 2 o'clock last night, in which two of the desperadoes were wounded, one probably mortally.

Gaffey gives your reporter the following account of their trip and fight: His posse consisted of John Royce, Tom Ritchie, L. Galindo and Jim Murphy. After the first day they followed a mountain trail to the New Almaden mines, arriving there almost worn out, and with their horses hardly able to take another step. The inn-keeper refused to sell them any hay, although he had plenty, and would not allow them to lodge there. They went to the Superintendent of the mines finally, and were by him permitted to sleep in the stables of the company. On the way over they searched every cabin on Uvas creek in Santa Clara county, and on their return they were informed by a Californian that they passed within a few hundred yards of their men in searching the houses on the creek, and that they were concealed by a man whose house they had searched, and who had declared he had not seen them in six months. They went immediately to this house, and told the owner to show them where the men were. It was then nearly 2 o'clock in the morning. He replied that he knew nothing of them. They then swung the man up until his tongue protruded, but still he refused to tell. Again they raised him, and when lowered he said he would tell them if they would not hang him. He took them to a small hut in the brush near by, and rushing in they found a man, but neither one of the men they were after. This man pretended ignorance, but when Royce, with a terrible oath, made a jump for him with the rope, he weakened, and said they were in a hollow tree near by. They were conducted to the spot and surrounded the tree. Gaffey approached, and attempting to look into the stump called out to them to surrender, if they were there. This nearly cost him his life, as he was answered by a pistol-ball, which just grazed his head. He then fired into the stump, wounding, as was afterwards developed, one of them, Ignacio Tejada, through the one of them, Ignacio Tejada.

Keating's store, in Castroville, about 9 o'clock this morning, they had an altercation, resulting in both men drawing pistols and clinching. A Fight With Muderers.
WATSONVILLE, Cal., January 10. — The residents of this place are greatly excited to-day over the news of an encounter that took place in the mountains last evening between a posse of police and two murderers named Ignacio Tijada and John Leal. The police pursued them into a thickly-wooded portion of the mountains and discovered them secreted in a hollow tree. As the police approached the murderers opened fire on them with revolvers. The police returned the fire until both men dropped their arms. They then rushed in on the pair and found that Leal was mortally wounded and Tijada shot through the body and suffering greatly. As the police passed through the town toward the jail with their prisoners they were followed by a mob, who threatened to lynch the prisoners.

TA CRUZ. January 21st - This
A Bad Man Sentenced.
SANTA CRUZ, January 21st.—This afternoon Judge Logan, in the Superior Court, sentenced Ygnacio Tejada, one of the gang recently captured by Under Sheriff Gaffey, concerned in the shooting of Charles Rossi, near Watsonville, to seven years in San Quentin. Tejada is a desperate character, and was only captured by Gaffey after being shot in the arm. The crime for which Tejada was sentenced was for shooting at one Jesus, an Indian, and for holding Deputy Sheriff Sylvar and allowing some prisoners to break jail seven years ago.

A Policeman Killed by a Woman at Fargo.
Policeman Alderman, of Fargo, was shot dead through the heart, Wednesday night, while in search of a prisoner who had been released during the day to obtain money to pay a fine inflicted for drunkenness. In his search for his man the officer rapped at the door of a house occupied by Mrs. Martin Bunkle, and upon being interrogated as to his name and business, Mrs. Bunkle opened the door and fired, the bullet taking effect in the officer's heart, resulting in instant death.
The woman gave herself up and confessed the deed, explaining that she supposed the man to be a tramp. Her husband when leaving home in the morning had given her the revolver, as tramps had been seen in the vicinity.
The coroner's jury returned a verdict of justifiable homicide, and the woman was discharged.

A horrible murder was discovered on the farm of Jno. Dustin, three miles south of Kewanee, Ill. Mrs. Maggie Copeland being left alone in the house while her husband and family went to town to do shopping, some man entered the house, knocked her down with a board, shot her twice through the body and crushed in her head with a club. One hundred and twenty-eight pension certificates were issued from the department in Washington the other day.

The committee that has been making an investigation into the management of the store-keepers' department of the treasury building have discovered that there has been a regular and systematic shortage in the amount of ice delivered at the Treasury Department extending over two years. The Treasury Department is secured by bond of Agent Knickerbocker, of the ice company, and will have the entire shortage refunded and covered back into the treasury.

Texas fever has attacked cattle at several slaughter houses on the outskirts of Auburn, N. Y. All the beef is sold under certificates of the Board of Health. The action of Gov. They were accompanied by his widow and escorted by a detail of four naval officers from Mare Island and Major Gen. McDowell and staff. The funeral took place on the island at 3 o'clock with naval honors, and was attended by all the naval officers stationed either here or there.

Chinese Statistics.

There are in this city 1400 Chinese women and girls of whom 1200 are concubines or prostitutes and all slaves. On one small alley in Chinatown a house contains over 100 Chinese prostitutes. The number of opium dens and gambling houses in San Francisco is not known even to the police authorities. Shot and Killed.

SONORA, Cal., Aug. 11.—About 6 o'clock on the 7th, on Mormon creek, near the mountain brow, Sol Haslem shot and killed Samuel Brooks with a double-barreled shotgun loaded with buckshot. Haslem and Brooks were both married men who live a short distance apart and have been enemies for a year. On Wednesday evening Brooks and Haslem had a quarrel. Shortly after, Brooks, who was slightly intoxicated, was going towards Haslem's house with a double-barreled shotgun in his hand. Haslem called from his house and told Brooks not to cross the bridge or he would kill him. Brooks paid no attention. When he crossed the bridge Haslem was standing in front of his house, and fired one shot at him, taking effect in the face and breast. Brooks made one or two steps forward, stooped and laid his gun down and fell upon it, and died in a few minutes. Reports differ as to who made the first threats. The Coroner held an inquest, and a verdict of unjustifiable homicide was rendered. The Deputy Sheriff searched Haslem's house and vicinity, but could not find his gun. Mrs. Haslem claims he has not had a gun for a year.

A Reign of Terror.

SAN FRANCISCO, Aug. 11.—Advices of the 8th from Hermosillo, Sonora, in Mexico, say that parties just arrived from Ures report Apache depredations in that section most fearful. Over 200 warriors are in the Mazatlan mountains near Ures, and are making daily raids on the valley in small bodies, burning crops and houses, and murdering the inhabitants. During the past twelve days forty-five pkrsons have been murdered within a radius of twenty five miles of Ures. Among the victims was Lorenzo Vallencia, a wealthy citizen of Ures, also prominent Government officials are among the murdered. Last week they attacked the Ranche Viega. The fight lasted four hours. Four of the ranchers were killed and the remainder wounden. Nine Apaches were left on the field. The approach of a body of Mexican troops caused their retreat. The Apaches are from San Carlos agency. All are armed with Winchester rifles, and use cartridges stamped U. S. The Mexicans are poorly armed with muzzle loaders. The country is terrorized, business is paralyzed and settlers are fleeing from their ranches to Ures. All available Mexican troops are being concentrated to operate against them.

Portland, Or., Aug. 14.—Particulars reached here this afternoon of a cold-blooded murder near Mollala cross roads, Clackamas County, on Saturday, by David Morris, a man about 50 years of age. David Morris and his nephew, Sterling Officer, aged 18, were returning home from Mollalla on horseback, and the conversation turned on Morris's son, who was a companion of young Officer's. Morris remarked that his son was bad at heart and incorrigible. Young Officer remarked that if this was so "it is your own fault, as you never managed the boy right." Sterling then dismounted to adjust the saddle or girth, when Morris jumped from his horse, drew a pocket knife, stepped to the boy's side, plunged the blade to the hilt inside of the neck, and drew it round to the front, severing the carotid artery and producing instant death. He then mounted his horse and rode home. Messengers came to Oregon City Saturday night, and informed the Sheriff, who went out and arrested Morris in bed. He was lodged in the Oregon City jail. Fears are entertained that friends of the dead boy will try to lynch Morris. The murderer is a farmer, much given to drink, and when under the influence of liquor is very quarrelsome and abusive.

ADDITIONAL POINTS ABOUT THE KILLING OF YOUNG ATKINSON—THE SUPPOSED MURDEKER MARRIED THE NIGHT BEFORE THE DASTARDLY DEED—WHO HE IS AND HOW HE WAS CAPTURED.

[Correspondence of the Richmond Dispatch.]

DANVILLE, VA., February 6, 1882.

Letters having come through on the Midland road after so long a time, additional information has been obtained about the killing of Atkinson; as it is supposed, by W. H. Yeatts (commonly called Ham. Yeatts), at Sycamore station, on the night of the 2d instant. Yeatts is the son of Major C. W. Yeatts, who was once commissioner of the revenue in one of the districts of this county, and he was once a tobacco commission merchant in Lynchburg in the firm of Yeatts & Steptoe. On the night before Atkinson was killed he was married to Miss Rorer, of this county. About ten days ago he presented to Atkinson a draft from T. L. Poindexter & Co., of the Public warehouse of this city, for $70, for which Atkinson gave him some money and some goods, which draft is now pronounced a forgery. A few days before the killing of Atkinson it is said he borrowed his pistol from him, and that he never returned it. When he shot Atkinson he was wearing a pair of rubber over-shoes. The pistol was put so close to the head that the hair was singed. After the shooting he went off with Atkinson's pistol, his pocket-book, and two rings taken from his fingers, and at Motley's station he got on the freight train for Lynchburg, and thence started off west. Atkinson was killed on the railroad-track, dragged to one side, and partly covered with logs. Near by where the body fell were the stumps of two cigars, which the parties are said to have been smoking when they set out from Sycamore station. The parties from whom I got my information know nothing about any old grudge between Atkinson and Yeatts. The wonder is what could have been his reason for killing Atkinson. ALPHA.

ADDITIONAL PARTICULARS.

The Lynchburg News of Sunday gives the following additional particulars: Fuller intelligence from the Pittsburgh homicide indicates that young Atkinson was murdered by W. H. Yeatts for purposes of robbery. It is said to have been known to the latter that his victim had in his possession as much as $800, and moreover that he was in the habit of carrying his money about his person. Yeatts is alleged to have tried to persuade the young merchant to accompany him on a trip to Lynchburg last Thursday morning; but Atkinson refusing, he called at his place of business, at Sycamore station, late that night, and invited him to take a walk. To this proposition the unsuspecting man assented, and the two were seen to leave the store, walking in the direction of this city. Soon after their departure the report of a pistol was heard, but this being of no unusual occurrence in that neighborhood, nothing was thought of it by persons at the station. The next morning, however, the station-hands on the railroad discovered the form of Atkinson lying near the side of the track with a bullet-hole through the head, and the body covered with heavy logs of wood, and his empty pocket-book lying near by.

Suspicion at once attached to Yeatts as the perpetrator of the foul crime, and when search discovered that he had disappeared these suspicions were confirmed, and the friends of the murdered man immediately communicated the facts of the occurrence to the police authorities of this city in the hope of bringing the assassin to justice.
Captain Pettigrew instituted an investigation without a second's delay, and, learning that a man of the description furnished had registered at the Relay House Friday night under the name of W. D. Wagan, and had left on the western-bound freight train early Friday morning for "some point beyond Tennessee," to employ the man's expression to the agent from whom he purchased his ticket, the officer immediately telegraphed to points along the road, and as a result of his persistent efforts Yeatts, or a man supposed to be him, was arrested early yesterday morning at Bristol just as he had boarded the East Tennessee, Virginia and Georgia passenger train.

Captain Pettigrew is satisfied that he has the right man, and dispatched Officer Gouldman to Bristol yesterday to fetch him back to this city, where he will be held in custody for the action of the Pittsylvania authorities.

Yeatts, a twenty-six-year-old son of Major Charles W. Yeatts, who was formerly a district internal-revenue collector, and also a commission merchant in Lynchburg, Va. Young Yeatts was thought to have been on terms of friendly and familiar intercourse with Adkerson, for it was known that the latter had often befriended him pecuniarily and in other ways. What pointed suspicion at Yeatts was the fact that he was married on February 1st (the day before the murder) to a Miss Fannie Rorer, who lived near Sycamore, and that on the next day he told his wife that he was going away for three weeks to work on the New-River railroad. He then left, and it appeared from after developments that he repaired to Sycamore, and by some representations induced Adkerson to take a walk with him up the railroad track towards Lynchburg. Shortly thereafter a pistol-shot was heard, but no attention was paid to the circumstance, as pistol-shooting thereabouts was no uncommon thing. The next morning, however,

ADKERSON'S BODY WAS FOUND
as described, with a hole through the head made by a bullet, which entered behind one ear and passed out near the other. The tracks about the murdered man, which plainly showed in the snow, were identified as those of Yeatts, and his sudden disappearance led to his being pursued. On the 5th of February he was arrested at Goodson-Bristol, on the Virginia and Tennessee border, and, though giving another name, was soon after identified by Pittsylvania county officers and brought back to the jail at Chatham; not, however, before the excited citizens of the neighborhood had made threats and some preparations to lynch the murderer. When arrested Yeatts was found in possession of Adkerson's pistol, safe-key, and two rings which he had taken from him after killing him. He also had some money which was believed to belong to his victim. His trial occurred at the May term of the County Court, and resulted in his conviction and sentence to be hanged on the 28th of July.

Among the representations which have been made in connection with the affair as showing the cause or

PROVOCATION FOR THE MURDER

is one that when Yeatts was engaged to Miss Rorer, Adkerson expressed regrets to her that she was going to marry a man who was dishonest, and who would after their marriage go to the penitentiary. The cause of this statement was due to the fact that Yeatts had passed on Adkerson for goods and money a bogus check for $75, to which the name of Thomas L. Poindexter & Co., of Danville, was forged, and that he had also tried to impose similar bogus paper on other business-men. It is also stated that Miss Rorer has sustained unlawful relations with Adkerson; that Yeatts knew it, and had been paid by Adkerson to marry the girl; and again, that he discovered her unchasteness only on marriage, and was led to suspect by remarks of Adkerson, who obtruded himself in the company of Yeatts and wife, that they had had guilty relations.

Whether Yeatts was moved to kill Adkerson by innate wickedness or from dread of punishment for committing the alleged forgeries, or from sudden fury at reflecting that Adkerson had been unduly intimate with his wife, must be left to conjecture.

A WEEK'S RESPIE.

A few days before, the day fixed by the Court for the execution of Yeatts his father submitted various papers to Governor Cameron, embracing evidence claimed to be of an extinguating character, accompanied by affidavits, which had not been introduced at the trial. The Governor therefore respited Yeatts for one week (until today), so that he could have time to look into the matter. After a careful investigation he decided not to interfere, but to let the law take its course.

For weeks before his trial he was besought by his counsel if he had any reason to suspect any undue intimacy between young Adkerson and his wife either before or after his marriage to speak out: in fact, they told him that the only way to save his neck from the gallows was to use some such argument, but he declared to the last that he had no ground for such a suspicion, and that young Adkerson was one of the best friends he ever had.

Yeatts's Last Confession.

Since his conviction, however, Yeatts has made two written confessions which conflict materially, as all his statements in connection with the murder have done. The last one he gave to Mr. L. H. Pigg, editor of the Chatham Tribune, with the request that it should not be made public until the day of his execution. In this he speaks of his intimate and friendly relations with Adkerson, the two having "lived together as brothers" for some time previous to his marriage.

On the Sunday before he was married he says: I went to Mr. Rorer's to see my intended wife, and while there she told me Mr. Adkerson had written a letter to her, in which he stated that I was living at Sycamore in danger, and that he was very sorry that she was going to marry me; that after marrying me I would have to leave her and go to the penitentiary for a forgery I had committed in signing Silverthorn's name to a paper which purported to pay me a large sum for a stone I had in my possession.

I remarked to her

I WOULD KILL HIM

unless he retracted for slandering me. I afterwards quieted down, and think I promised her not to say anything more about it. I went back to Sycamore that Sunday night, and as I had been given the privilege of going anywhere in the store as though it belonged to me, I went and armed myself with a large pistol which he left in the store.

On Monday morning we started together for Lynchburg, and directly after we boarded the train I went to him and demanded an explanation. Before I gave him a chance to reply I called him a damned scoundrel and told him he had been to Mr. Rorer's and taken advantage of me, and if he made the same statement to me that he did to them one or the other of us would have to die. He seemed to be very much surprised, and denied having said anything at all. I told him if that be so I retracted what I said about him. He insisted that he had said nothing against me, but that he was as good a friend as I had on earth. Upon this we settled the matter and went on as friends.
